description:
Worshipping Christ is not limited to standing before him or singing his praise. Continuing the discussion of how Christ satisfies his people, Wesam Saad explains indirect worship: delight in creation and relationships that leads to delight in their Creator. He begins with the present struggle over what the heart treasures. Work, possessions, comfort and even good gifts can compete with Christ when they become objects of ultimate devotion.

Romans 1 provides the contrast between recognising God through what he has made and worshipping the creature instead. Saad then considers the restored earth without that distortion. With sin removed, physical pleasures no longer distract from Christ; their beauty can reveal more of his goodness. He illustrates this with enjoying food, breathing freely, moving without pain and forming relationships without fear. These examples present a varied, embodied life of praise rather than one unending church meeting.

The study also connects rewards, generosity and different capacities for joy, while keeping Christ as the source of enjoyment. Its closing application is immediate: receive created blessings attentively, recognise what they reveal about Jesus, and invest present opportunities in faithfulness. The goal is to know Christ through his gifts without allowing the gifts to replace him.

questions.question: What does Saad mean by worshipping Christ indirectly?
questions.answer: He means enjoying created gifts in a way that draws attention and affection to their Creator. The beauty of a view, the pleasure of food or the gift of fellowship can reveal something of Christ’s goodness. The object of worship remains Christ, rather than the created thing being enjoyed.

questions.question: Why does the study describe worship as a constant activity?
questions.answer: Saad says the heart is continually treating something as worthy of devotion. That can be Christ, but it can also be money, personal security, comfort, reputation or another attachment. Attending worship or speaking praise therefore does not by itself prove that Christ is the heart’s supreme treasure throughout the week.

questions.question: How does Romans 1 shape the distinction between creation and Creator?
questions.answer: The study brings together creation revealing God’s attributes and people exchanging worship of the Creator for worship of creatures. Saad argues that created beauty is meant to direct attention to God. The problem lies in stopping at the gift and treating it as ultimate, rather than recognising the One whose character it displays.

questions.question: Why can a good blessing become a spiritual obstacle now?
questions.answer: Saad uses a home or job to illustrate how a gift can begin to govern decisions through fear of losing it. The same thing for which a believer gave thanks can compete with obedience or devotion to Christ. He presents these examples as an examination of the heart, rather than declaring every possession or employment decision sinful.

questions.question: How will enjoyment of creation differ in the restored earth?
questions.answer: In Saad’s explanation, sin will no longer distort enjoyment into rivalry with Christ. The pleasure of created gifts can therefore disclose more of his beauty without becoming an idol. The study expects physical life and relationships to be occasions for praise, rather than obstacles that must be escaped.

questions.question: How are rewards and generosity related to joy in this teaching?
questions.answer: Saad connects differing rewards with differing opportunities to enjoy Christ through his gifts, while saying that those with less will not be miserable. He also expects selfless sharing and relates the giver’s joy to the greater blessing of giving. These are his explanations of future enjoyment, not a numerical scale supplied by the session.

questions.question: What practice does the closing discussion encourage when we encounter beauty?
questions.answer: Rather than stopping at the pleasure of what is seen, listeners are encouraged to consider what it reveals about Christ. Saad sharpens this further: the aim is not merely to look away from the gift and say Jesus is better, but to learn more of his goodness through the created gift itself.

questions.question: Does the study picture heaven as one uninterrupted church meeting?
questions.answer: It distinguishes direct worship together from the many experiences through which Christ may be enjoyed indirectly. Saad describes meals, movement, conversation and relationships as illustrations of embodied praise. His imagined shops and arrangements are illustrative details, while the main point is a varied life whose pleasures continually direct attention to Jesus.
